s: interjection, a particle without an actual meaning, which is used in a conversation
conversation, chat, talk (conversing between people or parties, either for pleasure or for business)
Unsere Unterredung wurde jetzt im leichten Plauderton geführt wie ein harmloses Gespräch unter guten Bekannten.
Our discussion was now held in a light conversational tone like a harmless chat between friendly acquaintances.
Gespräch.et: From Middle High German gespræche, gesprēche, from Old High German gisprāchi, from Proto-Germanic *gasprakją. Cognates with Low German Gespreek, Hunsrik Gesprech, Luxembourgish Gespréich, Dutch gesprek, Old English gesprecan.

s: Ein Gespenst geht um in Europa – das Gespenst des Kommunismus.
A spectre is haunting Europe — the spectre of Communism.
Gespenst.et: From Middle High German gespenst, gespenste, from Old High German gispensti (“temptation, (devilish) illusion”), from spanan (“to lure, to attract”), with ghosts interpreted as "illusions that lure one away"; see the related spannen (“to stretch, span”) for fu…

s: 1924, Friedrich Bernhard Störzner, Das Torfgespenst, in: Reinhardtswalder Sagenbüchlein, Buchhandlung Otto Schmidt, page 17
At the peat banks it is uncanny at some times. Here, in dark nights, ghostly bluish lights scurry to and fro, who already scared and misguided many a walker.
interlocutor, collocutor (male or of unspecified gender) (A person who takes part in a dialogue or conversation)
Gesprächspartner.et: Gespräch (“conversation”) + -s- + Partner (“partner”). Cognate with Dutch gesprekspartner.

gesprächig.et: From Middle High German gespræchec, from Old High German gisprāhhīg. By surface analysis, Gespräch + -ig.

gespalten.et: From Middle High German gespalten, from Old High German gispaltan. Equivalent to ge- + spalten.

s: curious, excited (of a person; about seeing how something will turn out)
Ich bin gespannt, wie er das lösen wird.
I'm curious to see how he will solve that.

Gespan.et: From Middle High German gespan (“companion, comrade”), perhaps related to spannen.
Borrowed from Hungarian ispán, from a Slavic language.

s: a group of close partners, especially a pair of two
horse and cart, horse and carriage; oxcart
Gespann.et:
From Middle High German gespan (“clasp; frame, welt”), from Old High German gespan (“clasp; chain, bracelet”), from Proto-Germanic *ga- + *spannaną. Equivalent to ge- (collective prefix) + spannen (“to span, yoke”).
